en: The Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way, titled "Wisdom";
the Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way:
An Auspicious Invocation.
Neither ceasing nor arising, neither annihilated nor eternal,
not a unity nor a plurality, without coming and without going.
I pay homage to the Fully Awakened One, the best among speakers, who taught dependent origination— the auspicious stilling of conceptual proliferation.
1. An examination of conditions:
Never, anywhere, do any entities whatsoever exist as having arisen from themselves, nor from another, nor from both, nor without a cause.
There are four conditions: the causal condition, the objective condition, the immediate condition, and likewise the dominant condition; there is no fifth condition.
For the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of things does not exist in conditions and so forth;
since intrinsic nature does not exist, extrinsic nature (parabhāva) does not exist. //3//
Action does not possess conditions, nor is action devoid of conditions;
conditions do not possess action, yet they are indeed possessed of action. (4)
"These conditions are so called because [the effect] arises in dependence upon them.
As long as [the effect] has not arisen, how could these not be non-conditions? (5)
A condition is not logically possible for an object that is neither non-existent nor existent.
For what would a condition apply to if it were non-existent, and what need is there for a condition if it were already existent? (6)
When a phenomenon is produced neither as existent, nor as non-existent, nor as both existent and non-existent, how can a cause that produces it be logical under such circumstances? (7)
This very dharma, being existent, is taught as being without an object;
but if the dharma is without an object, how can there then be an object again? (8)
When phenomena have not arisen, cessation is not possible; therefore, an immediate [condition] is not logical. Furthermore, what condition could there be for that which has already ceased? (9)
Since there is no existence for things that lack intrinsic nature through their cultivation, the principle "this being, that comes to be" is simply not tenable. 10.
And that fruit does not exist in the conditions either individually or collectively;
how could that which does not exist in the conditions arise from the conditions? (11)
Now, if that which is non-existent arises from those conditions, why does the fruit not also arise from non-conditions? (12)
The fruit consists of conditions, yet the conditions themselves do not consist of themselves.
How can that fruit, which arises from things that do not consist of themselves, consist of conditions? (13)
Therefore, an effect consisting of conditions does not exist, nor one not consisting of conditions.
Since the effect is absent, how can there be conditions or non-conditions? (14)
2. An Examination of What Has Been Traversed, What Has Not Yet Been Traversed, and What Is Being Traversed:
That which has been traversed is not being traversed; likewise, that which has not yet been traversed is not being traversed.
Apart from what has been traversed and what has not yet been traversed, that which is being traversed is not being traversed.
Where there is movement, there is going; and that movement occurs in the path being traversed, not in what has already been gone over nor in what has not yet been reached.
Therefore, going exists in the path being traversed.
How indeed could the going of that which is being gone over be possible, when the going of that which is being gone over is not at all possible? (3)

For one who holds that there is going in the presently being gone over, it follows that there is a presently being gone over even without going, for the presently being gone over is indeed being gone over. 4.
If there were motion in that which is currently being traversed, two motions would follow:
that by which it is being traversed, and furthermore, the motion itself therein. (5)
If two acts of going were to occur, it would follow that there are two goers;
for indeed, an act of going is not possible apart from a goer. (6)
If going is not possible apart from a goer, then how indeed can there be a goer when going does not exist? (7)
First of all, the goer does not go; nor does the non-goer go.
Other than the goer and the non-goer, what third party could possibly go? (8)
How indeed can it be tenable that "the goer goes," when a goer without the act of going is not at all possible? (9)
For one who maintains the position that "the goer goes," it follows—contrary to reason—that there is a goer even without the act of going, since you desire the going to belong to the goer. (10)
If a goer goes, two acts of going would follow:
that by which he is designated as a "goer," and that which he, being a goer, performs. (11)
Going does not begin in what has already been gone over; going does not begin in what has not yet been gone over; it does not begin in the process of being gone over.
Where, then, does going begin?

Prior to the commencement of going, there is neither a path being traversed nor a path already traversed; where could going begin? For how can there be going in that which has not yet been traversed? (13)
When the commencement of going itself is not perceived in any way whatsoever, what is the gone, what is the being-gone-over, and what is the not-yet-gone that is conceptualized? 14.
The goer does not stand still, nor indeed does the non-goer stand still; what third party, other than the goer and the non-goer, could possibly stand still? (15)
How indeed could it be tenable that "the goer stands"?
For when a goer is not possible at all without the act of going, [how can he stand? (16)
Motion does not abide in that which is being traversed, nor in what has been traversed, nor even in what has not yet been traversed;
the commencement and cessation of motion are likewise identical to motion itself.
It is not tenable that the goer is the very same as the act of going;
nor is it tenable that the goer is something other than the act of going. (18)
For if the act of going were indeed identical to the goer, it would follow that the agent and the action are one and the same. (19)
If, on the other hand, the goer is conceptualized as being entirely distinct from the act of going, then there would be going without a goer, and a goer without going. (20)
For those two for whom establishment neither exists through identity nor through difference, how indeed could their establishment exist? (21)
By means of whatever going a goer is designated, he does not go by that very going;
for there is no one whatsoever who exists prior to going, since it is only someone [already] existing who goes. (22)
By means of whatever going a goer is designated, he does not go by any other;
for it is not possible for there to be two goings in a single goer. (23)
One who exists as a real entity does not go in the three ways of going;
nor does one who does not exist as a real entity go in the three ways of going. (24)
Going does not proceed in any of its three modes—as being existent, as being non-existent, or as being both;
therefore, motion, the goer, and the destination do not exist.
3. Examination of the Bases (Āyatana):
Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the mind—these are the six sense faculties; their respective objects are the visible and so forth. || 1 ||
For that vision does not see its own self;
since it does not see itself, how will it see others? 2.

The analogy of fire is not sufficient for the establishment of seeing; it has already been refuted along with "seeing" itself by means of the arguments concerning the traversed, the untraversed, and the being-traversed. ||3||
When there is no seeing whatsoever of that which is not being seen, how can it be tenable to say that "seeing sees"? ||4||
One does not see seeing at all, nor does one see non-seeing.
By means of seeing itself, the seer has also been explained; let it be understood in that same way. 5.
There is no seer apart from seeing, nor is there one who sees by means of seeing. Since the seer does not exist, how can there be that which is seen and seeing itself? (6)
Since there is no seeing of anything to be seen, the fourfold beginning with consciousness does not exist; how then will grasping and the subsequent factors come to be? (7)
Hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the mind have been explained;
one should understand the hearer, the object to be heard, and so forth, by means of sight alone. 8.
4. Examination of the Aggregates: Form is not perceived apart from the causes of form;
nor is the cause of form seen apart from form. (1)
If form were devoid of the cause that is form, it would follow that form is causeless;
yet no object whatsoever exists anywhere that is without a cause. (2)
If the cause of form were to exist apart from form itself, it would be a cause without an effect; yet there is no cause that lacks an effect. (3)
When form exists, a cause for form is not tenable;
when form does not exist, a cause for form is not tenable. (4)
Furthermore, form that is without a cause is simply not possible at all.
Therefore, one should not conceptualize any conceptual constructions regarding form. 5.
It is not tenable that the effect is similar to the cause;
nor is it tenable that the effect is dissimilar to the cause. (6)
The sequence for sensation, mind, perception, and mental formations is in every respect exactly the same as that for form; indeed, the process is identical for all phenomena whatsoever. (7)
If, during a debate, one should offer an avoidance by means of emptiness, then everything [the opponent has asserted] remains unrefuted; it becomes equal to that which is yet to be proven. (8)
If someone should offer an objection when an explanation based on emptiness has been given, everything that objection is unestablished, as it arises as being equal to the very point to be proven. (9)
5. Examination of the Elements: Space does not exist at all prior to the characteristic of space;
for if it were to exist prior to its characteristic, it would follow that it is without characteristics. (1)
Nowhere does any entity exist that is without characteristics; since an entity without characteristics does not exist, where could a characteristic possibly apply? (2)
The activity of a characteristic does not occur in that which is without characteristics, nor in that which possesses characteristics;
it does not proceed elsewhere than from both the characterized and the uncharacterized. (3)
And when the characteristic does not arise, the characterized object is not tenable;
and when the characterized object is not tenable, the characteristic itself is impossible. ||4||
Therefore, the characterized object does not exist, nor indeed does the characteristic exist;
apart from the characterized object and the characteristic, no entity whatsoever exists. (5)
And when an existent thing does not exist, of what will there be non-existence?
Furthermore, who—possessing the nature of both existence and non-existence—is there to perceive existence and non-existence? (6)
Therefore, it is neither existence nor non-existence, neither the characterized nor the characteristic;
space is like space, as are the other five elements. (7)
But those of small intelligence who perceive existence and non-existence do not see the auspicious tranquility of all things, which is the true object of vision. (8)
6. Examination of Passion and the One Attached to Passion:

If the one attached to passion existed prior to passion, being devoid of passion, then passion would exist in dependence upon him; thus, passion would exist only when the one attached to passion exists. (1)
Furthermore, if the one who is attached does not exist, how indeed will attachment come to be?
Whether attachment exists or does not exist, this same sequence applies to the one who is attached as well. (2)
Furthermore, the simultaneous arising of passion and the impassioned one is not logical;
for passion and the impassioned one would then exist independently of each other. (3)
In identity, there is no coexistence, for a thing cannot exist together with itself;
in difference, moreover, how could coexistence possibly occur? (4)
If coexistence were possible in identity, it would exist even without a companion;
if coexistence were possible in difference, it would exist even without a companion. (5)
If there were coexistence in separateness, what would be established regarding passion and the impassioned? If their parts were established as separate, then their coexistence would follow from that.
If the separate existence of passion and the impassioned one is established, for what purpose do you then imagine their coexistence? (7)
Thinking that it is not established as separate, you thus desire simultaneous existence;
yet for the sake of establishing simultaneous existence, you further desire separateness. (8)
And since separate existence is not established, co-existence is not established either. In the presence of what kind of separate existence do you desire co-existence? (9)
Thus, the establishment of passion through the impassioned is neither simultaneous nor non-simultaneous;
as with passion, so too is the establishment of all phenomena neither simultaneous nor non-simultaneous. 10.
7. Examination of Arising, Abiding, and Ceasing: If the conditioned exists, then the three characteristics [of arising, abiding, and ceasing] are applicable there.
But if arising were unconditioned, how could it be a characteristic of the conditioned? (1)

The three [characteristics], beginning with arising, taken individually, are not sufficient for the function of characterizing the conditioned; how could they exist together in one place at one time? (2)
If there exists another characteristic of the conditioned for arising, duration, and destruction, there would be an infinite regress; if it does not exist, then they are not conditioned. (3)
The arising of arising is merely the arising of the primary arising;
furthermore, the primary arising brings about the arising of arising. (4)
If, according to you, the "arising of arising" is the arising of the fundamental arising, how will that [secondary arising], which has not been produced by the fundamental [arising], produce it? (5)

If that [subsequent] fundamental [moment] produces a fundamental [moment], since it was produced by a fundamental [moment], how can that fundamental [moment], which was not yet produced by it, bring that [subsequent one] into existence? (6)
While arising, this [effect] might indeed produce that [cause], if this [effect], being unborn, were capable of producing that [cause]. (7)
Just as a lamp illuminates both itself and others, so too does origination bring about both itself and others. (8)
There is no darkness in a lamp, nor where it is established.
What does the lamp illuminate? For illumination is simply the destruction of darkness. (9)
How is darkness destroyed by a lamp that is in the process of arising?
For when the lamp is arising, it does not reach the darkness. (10)
Or if darkness were destroyed by a lamp without even reaching it, then a lamp staying here would destroy the darkness existing throughout the entire world. ||11||
If a lamp illuminates both itself and others, then darkness, too, will undoubtedly conceal both itself and others. (12)
How could this arising, being itself unarisen, produce its own self?
Or, if it produces [itself] once it has arisen, what is produced again when it is already born? (13)
Neither that which is presently arising, nor that which has arisen, nor that which has not yet arisen arises in any way;
this has been explained by means of the [analogy of] the present path, the traversed, and the untraversed. 14.
When this "presently arising" does not apply to the process of arising, how can one say that the presently arising arises in dependence upon arising? (15)
Whatever arises dependently is by its very nature quiescent;
therefore, that which is arising, as well as arising itself, is quiescent.
If some unarisen entity were found anywhere, it might arise; but since that entity does not exist, what is it that arises? 17.
If this arising, while itself arising, causes that which arises, then what other arising could it be that causes that arising? 18.
If another [production] produces this [production], there would be an infinite regress;
if, on the other hand, that which is unproduced is produced, then everything should likewise be produced in that manner. (19)
The arising of that which exists and that which does not exist is not tenable;
nor is it tenable for that which both exists and does not exist, as has already been demonstrated. (20)
The arising of an entity that is in the process of ceasing is not tenable;
nor is an entity that is not in the process of ceasing tenable. (21)
An entity that has not yet come to rest does not remain; an entity that has already come to rest does not remain.
That which is currently remaining does not remain; and what unarisen thing could possibly remain?
The persistence of an entity that is undergoing cessation is not tenable;
nor is an entity that is not undergoing cessation tenable. (23)
Since all entities always abide in the nature of aging and death, what entities are there that exist without aging and death? (24)
The abiding of abiding through another abiding, or through itself, is not tenable;
just as the arising of arising is neither through itself nor through another. (25)
That which has not ceased does not cease, nor does that which has already ceased cease;
likewise, that which is currently ceasing—how could that which is unborn cease? (26)
The cessation of an entity that is already established is not tenable; nor is the cessation of an entity that is not established tenable. (27)
Indeed, a state is not ceased by that very same state;
nor is a state ceased by a state that is other than itself. (28)
When the arising of all phenomena is not tenable, then likewise the cessation of all phenomena is not tenable. (29)
Furthermore, the cessation of an existent entity is not possible;
for if there were identity [between existence and non-existence], neither existence nor non-existence could be established. (30)
The cessation of a non-existent entity is not tenable, just as the cutting off of a second head does not occur. (31)
Cessation does not exist through its own nature, nor does cessation exist through another nature;
just as the arising of arising exists neither through itself nor through another. (32)
Since arising, abiding, and ceasing are not established, the conditioned does not exist;
and since the conditioned is not established, how will the unconditioned be established? (33)
Just as a magical illusion, just as a dream, and just as a city of the Gandharvas, so have arising, abiding, and passing away been described. (34)
8. Examination of Action and the Agent: A truly existent agent does not perform a truly existent action;
nor does a non-existent agent strive to perform a non-existent action. (1)
For that which is truly existent, there is no action, and there would be karma without an agent;
for that which is truly existent, there is no action, and there would be an agent without karma. (2)
If an unreal agent were to perform an unreal action, then the action would be without a cause, and the agent would also be without a cause. (3)
In the absence of a cause, neither effect nor cause exists;
in their absence, action, agent, and instrument do not exist. (4)
When actions and so forth are impossible, neither merit nor demerit exists;
and when merit and demerit do not exist, the fruit born from them does not exist. (5)
If the fruit did not exist, there would be no attainment of liberation nor of heaven;
furthermore, it would follow that all ritual actions are rendered purposeless. (6)
An agent who is both existent and non-existent does not produce that which is both existent and non-existent;
for how can the existent and the non-existent, being mutually contradictory, exist as one? (7)
That which is non-existent is not produced by that which exists, nor is that which exists produced by that which is non-existent;
for in that case, all those very same faults would necessarily follow for the agent. (8)
An agent does not perform an action that is non-existent, nor one that is existent, nor even one that is both existent and non-existent, for the reasons already stated. (9)
An agent who is non-existent does not produce an action that is existent, nor one that is both existent and non-existent; this is due to the very reasons previously stated. (10)
An agent who is both real and unreal does not perform an action that is real or unreal;
one should understand this by means of the very reasons already stated. 11.
Dependent upon the agent, the action occurs; and dependent upon that action, the agent occurs. We see no other cause for their establishment. 12.
Thus one should understand appropriation through the relinquishing of action;
and by means of both action and agent, one should analyze the remaining entities. (13)
9. Some indeed assert that there exists a grasper prior to grasping, as well as seeing, hearing, and so forth, and feeling and so forth.
For how could seeing and the other [sensory functions] belong to an entity that does not exist?
Therefore, prior to these [functions], that entity exists as established.
Furthermore, by what means can that entity which existed prior to seeing, hearing, and so forth, as well as feeling and so forth, be designated? (3)
If this [self] were established even without seeing and the other [faculties], then these too would undoubtedly exist without it. (4)
Someone is manifested by something; something is manifested by someone.
How can there be someone without something, and how can there be something without someone? (5)
No one exists prior to all [the functions] such as seeing;
rather, at different times, one [function] is manifested by means of another among seeing and the rest.
If it does not exist prior to all [the functions] such as seeing and so forth, how can it exist prior to each individual [function], such as seeing? (7)

If that very same one is the seer, that very same one is the hearer, and that very same one is the feeler, then [the self] would exist prior to each of these individually; however, this is not tenable. (8)
If the seer were one, the hearer another, and the knower yet another, then while there is a seer, there would also be a hearer, and there would be a plurality of selves. (9)
Furthermore, this [Self] does not exist even in those elements from which seeing, hearing, and so forth, as well as feeling and so forth, arise.
If that to which seeing, hearing, and so forth, as well as feeling and so forth belong, does not exist, then these [functions] do not exist either. (11)

That which exists prior to seeing and the other [sensory] functions, as well as now and in the future—regarding that, the conceptual constructions of "it exists" and "it does not exist" have ceased. (12)
10. Examination of Fire and Fuel:
If the fuel were the fire, there would be identity of the agent and the object;
if the fire were other than the fuel, it would exist even without the fuel.
It would be eternally aflame, having no cause for its ignition;
furthermore, in such a case, the act of starting it would be useless, and it would be devoid of action. ||2||
Because it would not depend on anything else, it would follow that fire is not caused by ignition;
furthermore, if it were eternally burning, its re-ignition would be purposeless. (3)
In this regard, it might be argued: "The fuel is that which is being ignited.
But by what is that fuel ignited, when it is merely that [fuel] itself? (4)
One who has not attained will not attain; one who does not burn will not burn again;
one who is not extinguished will not be extinguished, or else he will remain possessing his own characteristic mark.
If fire were indeed something other than fuel, it would reach the fuel, just as a woman reaches a man and a man reaches a woman. (6)
Fire would indeed be something other than fuel, and it might as well obtain the fuel, if fire and fuel were mutually independent of one another. (7)
If fire depends on fuel, and if fuel depends on fire, which of the two is established first, such that fire depends on it as fuel? (8)
If fire depends upon fuel, then it would be the establishment of a fire already established;
and if this were so, fuel too would exist without fire. (9)
If an entity is established in dependence upon another, and that very other is established in dependence upon it, then let that which is to be depended upon be established;
in dependence upon what, then, would what be established? (10)
How can an entity that is established in dependence upon something else be dependent while it is itself unestablished?
On the other hand, if it is already established, then its dependence is not logical. (11)
Fire does not exist in dependence on fuel, nor does fire exist without depending on fuel;
fuel does not exist in dependence on fire, nor does fuel exist without depending on fire. 12.
Fire does not come from elsewhere, nor is fire found within the fuel;
regarding this fuel, the rest has been explained by means of the analysis of what is being traversed, what has been traversed, and what has not yet been traversed. 13.
Furthermore, fuel is not fire, nor is fire other than fuel;
fire does not possess fuel, fuel is not in fire, nor is fire in them.
By means of fire and fuel, the sequence of the self and its appropriation has been explained entirely and without exception, along with [the analysis of] pots, cloths, and so forth. (15)
Those who point to a self and to the entities as being distinct from one another—I do not consider them to be experts in the meaning of the teaching. (16)
11. An examination of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*):
The Great Sage declared that no prior limit is known; for cyclic existence is indeed without beginning or end, having neither a first nor a last.
For that which has neither beginning nor end, how could there be a middle?
Therefore, in this case, sequences of prior, posterior, and simultaneous do not occur.
If birth were to exist first and old age and death afterwards, then birth would be without old age and death, and one who was immortal would be born. (3)
If birth were to occur later and old age and death were at the beginning, how could there be causeless old age and death for one who has not been born? (4)
Neither is aging-and-death joined with birth;
for if one were born and yet dying simultaneously, both would be without cause. (5)
Where these sequences of prior, posterior, and simultaneous do not prevail, how could they proliferate that birth, as well as its aging and death? (6)
Effect and cause, the characterized and the characteristic, sensation and the feeler—whatever objects there may be [are likewise non-existent]. (7)
Not only is a prior limit of cyclic existence not found, but for all phenomena as well, a prior limit is not found. (8)
12. Examination of Suffering:
Some maintain that suffering is self-created, created by another, created by both, or without cause; yet it is not logical for suffering to be an effect [in those ways].
If it were self-made, it would not arise dependently;
for indeed, these very aggregates arise in dependence upon those [prior] aggregates. (2)
If these were different from those, or if those were different from these, then suffering would be produced by another; for these [beings] would have been created by those others. (3)
If suffering were created by one's own person, then that person would exist without suffering; yet who is that person by whom the suffering was self-created? (4)
If suffering produced by another person is given to someone else after having been created by that other, how could that [recipient] exist without suffering [to give it]? (5)
If suffering is produced by another person, who is that other person who,
being himself free from suffering, creates it and sends it to another?
Since self-causation is not established, how can suffering be caused by another?
For if another were to inflict suffering upon him, that would be something done by himself.
Suffering is not first of all self-made, for it cannot be created by that very same [self];
nor is it made by another if that other were not himself self-made—so how could suffering be made by another? (8)
If suffering were produced by both [self and other], it would also have to be produced by each one individually;
how then could there be suffering that is neither caused by another nor caused by oneself, which would be without a cause? (9)
For not only does the fourfold nature of suffering not exist, but even the fourfold nature of external entities does not exist. 10.
13. Examination of Reality:
That which has the nature of deception is false, as the Blessed One has declared;
and since all conditioned phenomena have the nature of deception, they are therefore false.
If that which has the nature of deception is false, what is it therein that is deceived?
This was stated by the Blessed One as an illumination of emptiness. (2)
The lack of intrinsic nature in entities is due to the observation of their changing state;
for there is no entity that lacks intrinsic nature, since all entities are empty. (3)
If intrinsic nature does not exist, of what could there be alteration?
If intrinsic nature does exist, of what could there be alteration? (4)
Neither the change of that very thing nor of something else is tenable;
for it is not the youth that ages, nor is it the aged that ages. (5)
If there were a change of state in that [milk], then milk itself would become curd;
for what other thing besides milk could possibly become curd? (6)
If there were something non-empty, there might also be something empty;
but since there is nothing whatsoever that is non-empty, how will there be anything empty? (7)
Emptiness was proclaimed by the Victors as the relinquishing of all views;
but those for whom emptiness itself is a view were declared incurable. (8)
14. Examination of Connection:
The object of vision, the act of seeing, and the seer—these three do not enter into connection with one another either two by two or all together.
In this way, let passion, the impassioned one, and the object of passion be seen;
by means of these three, the remaining afflictions and the remaining sense-bases are also to be understood.
The association of one thing with another presupposes their difference;
however, since the objects beginning with "the visible" (draṣṭavya) do not enter into such association, that difference does not exist. || 3 ||
Not only does otherness not exist for the seer and so forth; otherness is not tenable for anything whatsoever in relation to anything else. (4)
One thing is dependent on another; one thing does not exist apart from another.
And that which is dependent upon something else cannot logically be other than that [upon which it depends]. (5)
If one thing were other than another, it would exist even without that other; yet that "other" does not exist without the other, and therefore it does not exist at all. (6)
Difference does not exist in that which is other, nor does it exist in that which is not other.
Since difference does not exist, there is neither "other" nor "that very thing. (7)
Neither its conjunction with itself nor the conjunction of one thing with another is possible;
for neither that which is being conjoined, nor that which has been conjoined, nor a conjoiner exists.
15. Examination of Being and Non-being:
It is not logical for an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) to arise from causes and conditions;
if it were produced by causes and conditions, that intrinsic nature would be something created. (1)
Furthermore, how could intrinsic nature (svabhāva) possibly be something produced?
For intrinsic nature is uncreated and independent of anything else. (2)
How can there be an other-nature (parabhāva) in the absence of self-nature (svabhāva)?
For self-nature is indeed said to be the other-nature of an other-nature. (3)
Apart from intrinsic nature and extrinsic nature, how could there be an entity?
For it is only when intrinsic nature and extrinsic nature exist that an entity is established. (4)
If existence is not established, non-existence is certainly not established;
for people describe non-existence as the alteration of existence. (5)
Those who perceive intrinsic nature and extrinsic nature, as well as existence and non-existence, do not perceive the reality in the Buddha’s teaching. 6.
And in the *Kātyāyanāvavāda*, both "it exists" and "it does not exist" were refuted by the Blessed One, who discerns both existence and non-existence. (7)
If existence were by way of intrinsic nature, its non-existence could not occur;
for a change in the state of intrinsic nature is never possible. (8)
If primordial nature (prakṛti) does not exist, of what could there be alteration?
Or, if primordial nature exists, of what could there be alteration? (9)
"It exists" is the grasping at permanence; "it does not exist" is the view of nihilism.
Therefore, the wise person should not rely upon either existence or non-existence. (10)
For that which exists by way of intrinsic nature cannot be non-existent; thus, eternalism follows.
To say "it does not exist now, though it existed previously" entails the consequence of nihilism. (11)
16. Examination of Bondage and Liberation:

If it is the conditioned factors (*saṃskāras*) that transmigrate, they do not transmigrate as permanent entities; nor do they transmigrate as impermanent entities. This same reasoning applies to a sentient being (*sattva*) as well.
If it is the person who transmigrates within the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements, that person cannot be found in five ways; since he does not exist, who is it that will transmigrate? (2)
Transmigrating from one grasping to another, one would become non-existent;
and being non-existent and without grasping, who is that person, and what is it that will transmigrate? (3)
The nirvāṇa of conditioned phenomena is not possible in any way;
the nirvāṇa of a sentient being is also not possible in any way. (4)
Formations, being subject to the nature of arising and passing away, are neither bound nor liberated; as before, the sentient being is neither bound nor liberated. (5)
If grasping is the bond, then one who possesses grasping is not bound; nor is one who lacks grasping bound. In what state, then, is one bound? (6)
One might indeed bind that which is being bound, if there were something prior to it to be bound;
but such a thing does not exist, as has been explained by the analysis of the traversed, the untraversed, and that which is being traversed.
One who is bound is not liberated, nor indeed is one who is unbound liberated.
If the bound were being liberated, there would be simultaneous bondage and liberation. (8)
"I shall attain nirvana without grasping; nirvana will be mine"—for those who hold such a view, this is a great grasping at clinging. (9)
There is no superimposition of nirvāṇa, nor any removal of saṃsāra.
Where [these do not exist], what is saṃsāra there, and what nirvāṇa is conceptualized? 10.

17. Examination of the Fruit of Action: That mental state which restrains oneself and benefits others, being characterized by loving-kindness—that is the Dharma; it is the seed of fruit both in this world and after death.
The Supreme Seer has declared that action consists of volition and what is performed after having willed;
he has fully described the manifold divisions of that action. ||2||
In that regard, what is called "volition" is known as mental action; and what is called "having willed" is both bodily and vocal action. (3)
The vibrations of speech and those non-abstinences designated as "non-informative" (avijñapti), as well as other abstinences, are likewise considered to be non-informative. (4)
Merit resulting from enjoyment and likewise demerit of that same kind, as well as volition—these seven factors are traditionally known as the manifestations of karma. ||5||
If the action remains until the time of ripening, it would attain permanence;
if it has ceased, being already ceased, how will it produce a fruit? (6)
The continuum beginning with the sprout that proceeds from the seed—from that [continuum] the fruit arises; and without the seed, that [continuum] does not proceed. (7)
Since the continuum arises from the seed, and the production of the fruit arises from the continuum, the fruit is preceded by the seed; therefore, it is neither annihilated nor eternal. (8)
The mental continuum which proceeds from that mind—from that [continuum] the fruit arises; and without the mind, that [continuum] does not proceed. (9)
Since the continuum arises from the mind, and the arising of the fruit occurs from the continuum, the fruit is preceded by karma; therefore, it is neither annihilated nor eternal. (10)
The ten white paths of action are the means for accomplishing dharma;
the fruit of dharma consists of the five strands of sensual pleasure both in this world and after death. (11)
If this hypothesis were true, there would be many and great defects;
therefore, this hypothesis is not at all tenable here.
Furthermore, I shall now declare this conceptualization which is applicable here, and which has been praised by the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas. (13)
Just as a promissory note is not lost, so too is karma like a debt;
it is fourfold according to its constituent elements, and by nature it is indeterminate.
It is not to be abandoned by the path of seeing, nor is it to be abandoned by the path of cultivation;
therefore, the fruit of actions arises through non-perishing. (15)
If [the fruit] were to be abandoned through the abandonment [of the action], or by the transference of the action, then faults such as the destruction of the action would follow. (16)
Upon the reintegration of all heterogeneous and homogeneous karmas along with their constituent elements, that single [rebirth] arises. (17)
That [result] arises in the present life from every kind of action;
furthermore, it remains even when the two-fold [action] has matured.
It ceases either through the transcendence of its fruit or through death;
therein one should discern the distinction between that which is with outflows and that which is without outflows. //19//
Emptiness is not annihilation, and cyclic existence is not eternal;
the non-perishing of karma—this is the Dharma taught by the Buddha. 20.
Why does karma not arise? Because it is without intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva).
And because it is unarisen, for that reason it does not perish. 21.
If karma were to exist by way of its own intrinsic nature, it would undoubtedly be eternal;
yet karma would then be uncreated, for that which is eternal is not produced. (22)
If action were uncreated, there would be the fear of encountering the results of what one has not done;
furthermore, the fault of not living the life of celibacy would follow in that case. (23)
All worldly conventions would undoubtedly be contradicted;
furthermore, the distinction between the doer of merit and the doer of evil would not be tenable.
Furthermore, that which has already ripened as its fruition would ripen yet again, because karma is established as being inherent by nature. (25)
This [world] consists of karma and afflictions, yet those afflictions do not exist in reality;
if those afflictions do not exist in reality, how could karma exist in reality? (26)
Karma and the afflictions are declared to be the conditions for bodies;
if karma and the afflictions are empty, what can be said of bodies? (27)
Enveloped by ignorance and bound by craving, that being is the enjoyer; yet he is neither different from the agent nor is he that very same person. (28)
Since this action neither arises from conditions nor is it produced without conditions, therefore the agent also does not exist. (29)
If there is no action and no agent, from where could the fruit born of action arise?
And if the fruit does not exist, how indeed will there be an enjoyer? (30)

Just as the Teacher, through his perfection of supernatural power, creates a magical emanation, and that emanation in turn creates another emanation, and that emanation again [creates yet another]. (31)
Likewise, the agent who performs that action has the form of a magical creation;
it is just as when one magical creation creates another magical creation. (32)
Afflictions, actions, bodies, agents, and fruits are like the city of the Gandharvas; they resemble a mirage or a dream. (33)
18. Examination of the Self and Phenomena: If the self were the aggregates, it would be subject to arising and passing away;
if it were other than the aggregates, it would lack the characteristics of the aggregates. (1)
When the self does not exist, how indeed can that which belongs to the self come to be?
Through the pacification of both the self and what pertains to the self, one is free from "mine-ness" and free from "I-ness. (2)
Even he who is without "mine-ness" and without egoism does not exist [as a real entity];
he who perceives one who is without "mine-ness" and without egoism does not truly perceive. ||3||
When "mine" and "I" have perished, both externally and internally, grasping ceases;
through the destruction of that, there is the destruction of birth. (4)

Liberation comes from the exhaustion of karma and afflictions; karma and afflictions arise from conceptual construction; these arise from mental proliferation; and mental proliferation ceases within emptiness. (5)
The Buddhas have designated "self," they have taught "non-self," and they have also taught that there is neither self nor non-self at all. (6)
That which is to be expressed has ceased, and the range of the mind has ceased;
for the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is indeed unarisen and unceasing, like nirvāṇa. //7//
"All is real, or all is not real, or all is both real and unreal, or all is neither unreal nor real—this is the instruction of the Buddhas. (8)
Not dependent on another, peaceful, not elaborated by conceptual proliferations, free from discursive thought, and without manifold meanings—this is the characteristic of reality. 9.
Whatever arises dependently is not indeed that very thing, nor is it something other than it;
therefore, it is neither annihilated nor eternal. 10.
Neither of one meaning nor of many meanings, neither annihilated nor eternal—this is the nectar-like teaching of the Buddhas, the Lords of the World. 11.
When the Perfectly Enlightened Ones have not appeared and the Śrāvakas have passed away, the knowledge of the Pratyekabuddhas arises from solitude. 12.
19. Examination of Time:
If the present and the future exist in dependence upon the past, then the present and the future would both exist within the time of the past. (1)
If, moreover, the present and the future do not exist there [in the past], how could the present and the future exist in dependence upon it? 2.
Furthermore, the establishment of those two does not exist without depending on the past;
therefore, neither the present nor the future time exists. (3)

By this very same method, one should characterize the two remaining types of exchange (parivartaka) in their respective order—the superior, inferior, and middling, as well as unity and so forth. ||4||
Time that is not abiding cannot be grasped; time that is abiding does not exist.
How can time be designated when it is neither being grasped nor has been grasped? (5)
If time exists dependent upon an entity, how can there be time apart from an entity?
Since no such entity exists at all, how will time come to be? (6)
20. Examination of Causes:
If the effect arises from the assemblage of causes and conditions, and if that effect already exists within the assemblage, how can it be said to arise from the assemblage?
If the fruit arises from the assemblage of causes and conditions, and yet that fruit does not exist within the assemblage, how can it arise from the assemblage? (2)
If the effect existed within the assemblage of causes and conditions, it would surely be perceived within that assemblage; yet it is not perceived within the assemblage. (3)
If the effect does not exist within the assemblage of causes and conditions, then those causes and conditions would be equivalent to non-causes and non-conditions. (4)
If the cause, having given its causal efficiency to the fruit, were then to cease, there would be a twofold nature of the cause: that which has been given and that which has ceased. (5)
And if the cause were to cease without having imparted its causal efficiency to the fruit, then that fruit, being born when the cause has ceased, would be without a cause. (6)
If, moreover, the fruit were to manifest simultaneously with the causal complex, it would follow that the producer and that which is produced exist at the same time. (7)
Furthermore, if the fruit were to manifest prior to the causal complex itself, then the fruit would be devoid of causes and conditions, and thus would be causeless. (8)
If the fruit were to exist when the cause has ceased, there would be a transference of the cause;
furthermore, it would follow that a cause already previously born would be born again. (9)
How could a cause that has ceased and passed away produce an arisen effect?
And how could a cause, even while persisting, produce an effect when it is enveloped by it? (10)
Furthermore, if this [cause] were unobstructed by its fruit, what kind of fruit could it produce?
For a cause does not produce a fruit either by not seeing it or by having seen it. (11)
For a past effect, there is never any conjunction with a past cause, nor with one that is unborn, nor with one that has already arisen. (12)
For there is never any conjunction of an arisen effect with an unarisen cause, nor with one that has passed away, nor with one that is currently arising. (13)
For an unarisen effect has no conjunction whatsoever with an arisen cause, nor with one that is unarisen, nor with one that has perished. (14)
If there is no conjunction, how can a cause produce an effect?
Or, if there is a conjunction, how can a cause produce an effect? (15)
If the cause is empty of the effect, how can it produce the effect?
If the cause is not empty of the effect, how can it produce the effect? (16)
A non-empty fruit will not arise, and a non-empty one will not cease.
That which is non-empty would thus be neither ceased nor arisen. 17.
How could that which is empty arise? How could that which is empty cease?
It follows that even the empty would be unceasing and unarisen. 18.
For the identity of cause and effect is never logically tenable.
For the distinctness of cause and effect is never logically tenable. ||19||
If cause and effect were identical, there would be oneness between the producer and the produced;
if cause and effect were distinct, the cause would be equivalent to a non-cause. (20)
How can a cause produce an effect that exists by way of its own intrinsic nature? How can a cause produce an effect that does not exist by way of its own intrinsic nature? (21)
And for that which does not produce [an effect], the status of being a cause is not tenable;
and when the status of being a cause is untenable, whose will be the fruit? (22)
Furthermore, how could that very collection of conditions and causes, which by itself produces its own self, produce an effect? (23)
Therefore, the fruit is neither produced by a causal complex nor produced by what is not a causal complex;
for how could there be a causal complex in the absence of a fruit? (24)
21. An Examination of Origination and Dissolution:
Dissolution does not exist either apart from or together with origination;
origination likewise does not exist either apart from or together with dissolution. (1)
How indeed could there be dissolution without origination?
There can be no death without birth; dissolution does not exist without emergence. (2)
How can arising and passing away exist simultaneously?
For birth and death are never found at the same time. (3)
How indeed could there be arising without passing away?
For impermanence is never not found among existing things. (4)
How can arising exist together with passing away?
For birth and death are never found to occur at the same time. (5)
For those two for whom accomplishment does not exist either through mutual dependence or without mutual dependence, how indeed could their accomplishment possibly exist? (6)
There is no arising of that which is subject to destruction, nor is there the arising of that which is not subject to destruction;
there is no dissolution of that which is subject to destruction, nor is there the dissolution of that which is not subject to destruction. (7)
Neither origination nor destruction exists without existence;
neither existence nor destruction exists without origination and destruction. (8)
Neither arising nor passing away is possible for that which is empty;
neither arising nor passing away is possible for that which is non-empty. 9.
It is not tenable that origination and dissolution are one;
nor is it tenable that origination and dissolution are different. (10)
Both arising and passing away are seen by you;
yet it is through delusion that both arising and passing away are perceived. 11.
An existent does not arise from an existent, nor does an existent arise from a non-existent;
a non-existent does not arise from a non-existent, nor does a non-existent arise from an existent. 12.
An entity is not born from itself, nor is it born from another;
it is not born from both itself and another—how then could it be born? 13.
For one who accepts the existence of an entity, the views of eternalism or nihilism necessarily follow;
for that entity must be either permanent or impermanent. (14)
For one who has accepted [the existence of] becoming, there is neither annihilation nor permanence;
for that becoming is the continuum of the arising and passing away of cause and effect. //15//

If that existence (bhava) were a continuum of the arising and passing away of cause and effect, it would follow that there is a total cessation of the cause, because what has passed away does not arise again. ||16||
It is not logical for non-existence to exist by way of its own nature;
furthermore, at the time of nirvāṇa, there would be annihilation due to the cessation of the continuum of existence. (17)
The first existence is not tenable when the last has ceased, nor is the first existence tenable when the last has not ceased. (18)
If the first were to arise while the last is ceasing, then one would be in the process of ceasing and the other would be in the process of arising. (19)
If it were not the case that the one undergoing cessation and the one undergoing birth are joined together, then one would be born in those very same aggregates in which one dies. (20)
Thus, the continuity of existence is not tenable in any of the three times;
how can that which does not exist in the three times be a continuity of existence? (21)
22. Examination of the Tathāgata: The Tathāgata is not the aggregates, nor is he other than the aggregates; the aggregates are not in him, nor is he in them.
The Tathāgata does not possess the aggregates; who, then, is the Tathāgata here? (1)

If the Buddha does not exist by way of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) in dependence upon the aggregates, how could he exist by way of extrinsic nature (parabhāva), given that he does not exist by way of intrinsic nature? (2)
It is logically established that he who exists in dependence upon another nature is not the self;
and how can that which is not the self be the Tathāgata? (3)
If intrinsic nature does not exist, how could extrinsic nature exist?
Apart from intrinsic nature and extrinsic nature, who is that Tathāgata? (4)
If some Tathāgata were to exist without depending upon the aggregates, he would now have to depend [on them]; therefore, he would exist by means of dependence. (5)
Furthermore, there is no Tathāgata whatsoever who exists without depending upon the aggregates; and how can that which does not exist without depending [on them] ever take up those aggregates? (6)
There is no appropriation whatsoever that is not appropriated, nor does a Tathāgata exist in any way whatsoever without appropriation. (7)
How can that Tathāgata be designated by means of appropriation, when he does not exist as either identical to or different from [the aggregates], even when sought in five ways? (8)
Even this appropriation does not exist by way of intrinsic nature;
and that which does not exist by way of intrinsic nature, how could it exist by way of extrinsic nature? (9)
Thus, appropriation and the appropriator are entirely empty;
how can a Tathāgata, who is himself empty, be designated by means of that which is empty? (10)
"One should not say 'it is empty,' nor that 'it is non-empty'; one should not say it is both, nor that it is neither. It is spoken of only for the purpose of conventional designation. (11)
How can the fourfold set of views beginning with "eternal" and "non-eternal" exist in that which is peaceful?
And how can the fourfold set beginning with "finite" and "infinite" exist in that which is peaceful? (12)
He who has grasped the dense misconception that the Tathāgata exists, while conceptualizing that he does not exist, would likewise conceptualize [him] even when he has entered final nirvāṇa. (13)
Since this [Buddha] is empty by nature, the thought that "the Buddha exists after cessation" or "he does not exist" is simply not tenable. (14)
Those who conceptualize the Buddha, who is beyond conceptual proliferation and undecaying, are all destroyed by their own conceptualization and do not see the Tathāgata. 15.
Whatever is the nature of the Tathāgata, that is the nature of this world;
the Tathāgata is without intrinsic nature, and this world is without intrinsic nature. 16.
23. Examination of Error: Passion, hatred, and delusion are said to originate from conceptual construction;
for they arise in dependence upon the errors regarding the beautiful and the ugly. (1)
Those [afflictions] which arise in dependence upon the beautiful, the ugly, and the distortions do not exist by way of intrinsic nature; therefore, the afflictions do not exist in reality. (2)
The existence and non-existence of the self are not established in any way whatsoever;
without that [self], how could the existence and non-existence of the afflictions be established? (3)
For these afflictions belong to someone, yet that someone is not established;
or rather, do the afflictions exist for no one at all? (4)
As with the view of a self-body, the afflictions do not exist in the afflicted in five ways;
as with the view of a self-body, the afflicted also does not exist in the afflictions in five ways. (5)
Intrinsic nature does not exist for the errors of purity and impurity; dependent upon what [errors] would the afflictions arise? //6//
Visible forms, sounds, tastes, tangibles, odors, and mental phenomena—these sixfold objects are conceptualized as being associated with passion, hatred, and delusion. (7)
Forms, sounds, tastes, touches, smells, and mental objects alone are like the city of the Gandharvas, resembling a mirage or a dream. (8)
How could there be either impurity or purity in those who are like illusory persons and equal to reflections? (9)

Without depending on the beautiful, the ugly does not exist; that which we designate as "beautiful" exists only in dependence [upon the other], and therefore the beautiful is not established at all. (10)
Without depending on the impure, we could not designate the pure;
since it exists in dependence upon the impure, therefore the pure does not exist at all. (11)
And when the pleasant does not exist, from where will passion arise?
And when the unpleasant does not exist, from where will aversion arise? (12)
If the grasping at the impermanent as permanent is a misconception, since nothing impermanent exists in emptiness, how can there be such a grasping or misconception? (13)
If grasping at the impermanent as permanent is a misconception, why is grasping even at "impermanent" not a misconception regarding the empty? (14)
That by which one grasps, that which is the grasping, the grasper, and that which is grasped—all these are utterly stilled; therefore, no grasping exists. 15.
When grasping does not exist—whether it be false or even correct—to whom would there be error, and to whom would there be non-error? (16)
Furthermore, errors do not occur for one who is already mistaken, nor do errors occur for one who is not mistaken. (17)
Errors do not occur for one who is already in error; reflect for yourself as to whose errors could possibly occur. 18.
How indeed could inversions exist if they are unarisen? If inversions have not been born, how can there be one who possesses inversions? (19)
An entity is not born from itself, nor is it born from another;
it is not born from both itself and another—how, then, could one who has fallen into error [be established]?
(20) If the self, purity, permanence, and bliss were to exist...
And the self is pure, eternal, and blissful; there are no inversions [of these qualities]. ||21||
If neither a self, nor purity, nor permanence, nor happiness exists, then neither a non-self, nor impurity, nor impermanence, nor suffering exists either. 22.
In this way, ignorance ceases through the cessation of its misconceptions;
when ignorance has ceased, the formative forces and the rest cease. (23)
If any afflictions indeed existed for anyone by way of intrinsic nature, how could they possibly be abandoned? Who can abandon intrinsic nature? (24)
If any afflictions whatsoever were non-existent by way of intrinsic nature for anyone, how indeed could they be abandoned? Who would abandon that which has no real existence? (25)
24. Examination of the Noble Truths:
If all this is empty, there is neither arising nor passing away;
it follows that for you, the four noble truths do not exist. (1)
Full comprehension, abandonment, cultivation, and realization would not be possible, because of the non-existence of the four noble truths. (2)
In the absence of that, even the four fruits do not exist;
and in the absence of the fruits, there are neither those who abide in the fruits nor those who have entered toward them. (3)
If those eight types of persons do not exist, then the Saṅgha does not exist;
and due to the non-existence of the Noble Truths, the True Dharma also does not exist. (4)
If the Dharma and the Saṅgha do not exist, how can there be a Buddha?
By speaking thus, you contradict all three jewels. (5)
By [asserting] emptiness, you subvert the existence of the fruits [of action], as well as non-dharma and dharma itself, and all worldly conventional transactions. (6)
To this we reply: You do not understand the purpose of emptiness, nor emptiness itself, nor the meaning of emptiness; therefore you are thus frustrated. (7)
The teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas relies upon two truths:
the conventional truth of the world and the truth that is ultimate. (8)
Those who do not understand the distinction between these two truths do not understand the reality within the profound teaching of the Buddha. (9)
Without relying on conventional practice, the ultimate truth is not taught;
without attaining the ultimate truth, nirvāṇa is not realized. (10)
Emptiness, when wrongly perceived by those of dull intellect, destroys them, just as a snake wrongly grasped or a spell poorly executed [brings ruin]. (11)
And for this reason, the Sage turned his mind away from teaching the Dharma, considering that this Dharma is difficult for the dull-witted to fathom. (12)
Furthermore, whatever objection you raise regarding emptiness, that consequence of a fault does not apply to us in the case of the empty. 13.
Everything is possible for him for whom emptiness is possible;
nothing is possible for him for whom emptiness is not possible. 14.
Casting your own faults upon us, you have indeed mounted a horse, yet you have forgotten the horse itself. 15.
If you perceive the existence of things by way of their intrinsic nature (svabhāva), then you likewise perceive those things as being without causes and conditions. 16.
You negate the effect and the cause, as well as the agent, the instrument, and the action; you negate arising and ceasing, and the fruit as well. ||17||
That which is dependent origination, we declare to be emptiness;
it is a dependent designation, and it is itself the middle way. 18.
No phenomenon whatsoever exists that is not dependently originated;
therefore, no phenomenon whatsoever exists that is not empty. 19.
If all this were non-empty, there would be neither arising nor passing away;
it follows, therefore, that for you there would be the non-existence of the four noble truths. (20)
How could that which is not dependently originated be suffering?
For it has been stated that what is impermanent is suffering, and that does not exist in the case of intrinsic nature. 21.
How could that which exists by way of intrinsic nature ever arise?
Therefore, for one who contradicts emptiness, there is no origination. 22.
The cessation of suffering that exists by way of its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is not possible;
by asserting the existence of intrinsic nature, you obstruct cessation. 23.
If the path possesses intrinsic nature, its cultivation is not tenable;
yet if that path is cultivated, it lacks intrinsic nature for you. (24)
When suffering, its origin, and its cessation do not exist, what path, by virtue of being the cessation of suffering, will bring about [liberation]? (25)
If there is non-comprehension by way of intrinsic nature, how can there be comprehension of it again? For indeed, intrinsic nature is said to be eternally established. (26)
In this same way, for you, abandonment, realization, and cultivation are not tenable, nor are the four fruits, just as in the case of thorough knowledge. || 27 ||
How could that fruit which is not attained by way of intrinsic nature ever be attained again by one who grasps at intrinsic nature? (28)
In the absence of the fruits, there are none who abide in the fruits, nor are there any who have entered toward them;
if those eight types of persons do not exist, the Saṅgha does not exist. (29)
And because the noble truths do not exist, the true Dharma also does not exist.
When the Dharma and the Saṅgha do not exist, how will there be a Buddha? (30)
It would follow, according to you, that awakening exists even without depending on a Buddha;
and it would follow, according to you, that a Buddha exists even without depending on awakening. (31)
And he who is by nature unawakened, even though striving for awakening, will not attain awakening through the conduct of a bodhisattva. (32)
And no one will ever perform either dharma or adharma; for what can be done with that which is non-empty? Indeed, intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is not something that is produced. //33//
Indeed, for you there exists no fruit without dharma and adharma;
nor does a fruit caused by dharma and adharma exist for you.
Or if you hold that there is a fruit caused by merit and demerit, how can that fruit produced from merit and demerit be non-empty? (35)
And you contradict all worldly conventions, you who contradict emptiness as dependent origination. (36)
Nothing would need to be done, and no action would ever be undertaken;
one who negates emptiness would be an agent without acting. (37)
The world will be unarisen, unceased, and immutable;
though it appears through various states, it is devoid of intrinsic nature. (38)
The attainment of what has not yet been attained, the action that brings an end to suffering, and the abandonment of all afflictions—none of these exist if things are not empty. (39)
He who sees dependent origination sees this:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path itself. (40)
25. Examination of Nirvana:
If all this is empty, there is neither arising nor passing away;
through the abandoning or the cessation of what, then, is nirvana intended?
If all this were non-empty, there would be neither arising nor passing away;
through the abandoning or the cessation of what, then, is nirvana sought? (2)
Neither abandoned nor attained, neither annihilated nor eternal, neither ceased nor arisen—this is called nirvāṇa. //3//
Nirvāṇa cannot be an existing entity, for it would follow that it possesses the characteristics of aging and death; indeed, there is no existing entity that exists without aging and death. (4)
And if nirvana were an entity, then nirvana would be conditioned;
for no entity whatsoever exists anywhere that is unconditioned. (5)
And if nirvāṇa were an existent thing, how could it be non-dependent?
For indeed, no existent thing whatsoever exists that is not dependent. (6)
If nirvāṇa is not an existent thing, how will it be a non-existent thing?
Where there is no existent thing in nirvāṇa, there a non-existent thing is also not found. (7)
If nirvāṇa were a non-entity, how could it be non-dependent?
For there exists no such thing as a non-entity that occurs without dependence. (8)
That which is the state of coming and going, whether by way of grasping or dependent origination—that, when without grasping and not dependently originated, is taught as nirvāṇa. (9)
The Teacher has declared the abandonment of both existence and non-existence;
therefore, it is logical that nirvāṇa is neither existence nor non-existence. (10)
If nirvāṇa were both existence and non-existence, then liberation would be both existence and non-existence; and that is not tenable. 11.
If nirvāṇa were both existence and non-existence, then nirvāṇa would not be non-dependent, for it would depend upon both. 12.
How could nirvāṇa be both existence and non-existence?
For nirvāṇa is unconditioned, whereas existence and non-existence are conditioned. (13)
How could nirvāṇa be both existence and non-existence?
For the absence of these two in a single place is impossible, like that of light and darkness. (14)
The teaching that "nirvāṇa is neither non-existence nor existence" is established only if both existence and non-existence are themselves established. (15)
If nirvāṇa exists as neither non-existence nor existence, by what means is it characterized as "neither non-existence nor existence"? (16)
It cannot be asserted that the Blessed One exists after cessation;
nor can it be asserted that he does not exist, or both, or neither. (17)
Even while remaining, the Blessed One is not designated as "existing";
nor is he designated as "not existing," or "both," or "neither. || 18 ||
There is no distinction whatsoever of saṃsāra from nirvāṇa;
there is no distinction whatsoever of nirvāṇa from saṃsāra. (19)
The limit of nirvana and the limit of samsara—between these two, not even the slightest difference is found. (20)
Views concerning the end after cessation, such as those regarding the finite and so forth, or the eternal and so forth, are based upon nirvāṇa, the future limit, and the past limit. (21)
Since all phenomena are empty, what is infinite? What is finite?
What is both infinite and finite? And what is neither infinite nor finite? 22.
Is it that very thing, or is it something else? Is it eternal, or is it non-eternal?
Or is it both non-eternal and eternal, or perhaps neither of the two? (23)
The cessation of all apprehension, the cessation of conceptual proliferation, is peace.
Nowhere, to no one, has any dharma been taught by the Buddha. //24//
26. Examination of the Twelve Links:
One who is obscured by ignorance forms three types of volitional formations for the sake of renewed existence;
through those karmic actions, one goes to a state of rebirth. (1)
Consciousness, conditioned by formative forces, descends into the [new] state of existence;
once consciousness has descended, name-and-form is infused. 2.
When name-and-form has been infused, the six sense bases arise;
having reached the six sense bases, contact comes into being. (3)
Depending upon the eye, and form, and attention as well, consciousness thus proceeds depending upon name-and-form. (4)
The conjunction of these three—the eye, form, and consciousness—is contact; from that contact, feeling arises. (5)
Craving has feeling as its condition; for one craves for the sake of feeling. While craving, one grasps at the fourfold grasping. (6)
When there is grasping, existence proceeds for the grasper.
For if one were without grasping, one would be liberated and existence would not come to be. (7)
Those five aggregates are existence; from existence, birth proceeds, along with old age, death, suffering, and the like, as well as grief and lamentation. (8)
From birth proceed mental distress and despair;
thus occurs the arising of this entire mass of suffering. (9)

Because the ignorant person constructs the formative forces (saṃskāra), which are the root of saṃsāra, the ignorant one is therefore the agent; the wise one is not, because of his vision of reality. 10.
When ignorance has ceased, there is the non-arising of volitional formations;
the cessation of ignorance, however, results from the cultivation of this very knowledge. 11.
Through the cessation of each respective [condition], that very [effect] does not proceed;
in this way, this entire mass of suffering is completely extinguished. (12)
27. Examination of Views:
The views that "I did not exist in the past" and so forth—those views concerning the eternity of the world and others which rely upon the prior limit [of existence]. (1)
"Shall I not exist? Will there be another in the future time?"—such views as "I shall exist" and so forth are based upon the posterior limit. (2)
"It was not so in past time"—this is not tenable;
for he who existed in previous births is not this very same person. (3)
If it were the case that "that very [appropriation] is the self," then appropriation would be distinguished [as the self].
But then, what indeed is your self when it is entirely devoid of appropriation? (4)
If it is maintained that there is no self apart from the appropriation, then the appropriation itself would be the self; yet for you, there is still no self. (5)
Nor is the appropriation itself the self, for that [appropriation] passes away and arises again.
How indeed could the appropriation be the appropriator? (6)
Furthermore, a self that is distinct from the appropriation is not at all tenable; for if it were distinct, it would be perceived without appropriation, yet it is not so perceived. (7)
Thus, the self is neither other than the appropriations nor is it the appropriation itself;
there is no self that is without appropriation, yet it is not the case that it does not exist—this is the certainty. (8)
"It did not exist in past time"—this is not tenable;
for this [person] is not other than that [person] in previous births. (9)
For if this [self] were other [than the body], it would exist even after rejecting that [body];
likewise, it would remain there and would be born as immortal.
There would follow such consequences as the annihilation of actions, the destruction of karma, and that one person would experience the results of karma performed by another. (11)
Nor has it arisen after not having existed, for in that case the fault would follow that the self is either something produced or that it has arisen without a cause. (12)
Thus, regarding the past, the view that "I existed," "I did not exist," "both," or "neither" is not tenable. (13)
The view "Shall I exist in the future time?
and "Shall I not exist? are identical to [the views] regarding the past time. (14)
If that being were both a god and a human, it would be eternal;
yet a god would be unproduced, for that which is eternal is not born. (15)
If the human were different from the divine, then there would be impermanence;
if the human were different from the divine, then continuity would not be possible. 16.
If one part were divine and another part human, it would be both eternal and non-eternal; and that is not tenable. ||17||
If both the non-eternal and the eternal were established, then indeed the eternal would be established, as would the non-eternal. (18)
If someone who has come from somewhere were to go again to somewhere else, then [the self] would be beginningless and eternal; yet such a person does not exist. (19)
If nothing eternal exists, what could there be that is non-eternal?
Nor can there be anything both eternal and non-eternal, nor anything distinct from these two. (20)
If the world were finite, how could there be a future life?
And if the world were infinite, how could there be a future life? (21)
Since this continuity of the aggregates is like that of the flame of a lamp, therefore neither infinity nor finitude is tenable. 22.
If these aggregates were to perish in the past and yet these [present] aggregates were not to arise in dependence upon those [past] aggregates, then the world would be finite. (23)
If these aggregates were not destroyed in the past, nor were they produced, then this world would be infinite by virtue of depending upon these aggregates. (24)
If one part were finite while another part were infinite, then the world would be both finite and infinite; but that is not tenable. (25)
How, first of all, could one part of the appropriator perish while another part does not perish? This is not tenable. (26)
How indeed could one part of the appropriation perish while another part does not perish? This too is not tenable. (27)
If both the finite and the infinite were established as real, then it would be established that neither the finite nor the infinite exists, as you desire. (28)
Alternatively, since all entities are empty, where, for whom, which, and from what cause could views such as eternalism and the rest possibly arise? (29)
I pay homage to that Gautama who, out of compassion, taught the true Dharma for the sake of abandoning all views. (30)
